where: Section 1, first step of the numbered list
problem: The step 'Check aₙ > 0 and ratio limit 1' reads as if the ratio limit must equal 1 for Raabe's test to be legal. The only hypothesis of the test is aₙ > 0; ρ = 1 is just the situation in which the ratio test has already failed and Raabe's test becomes useful. A student may wrongly reject a valid Raabe computation when ρ ≠ 1.
fix: Check aₙ > 0. Raabe's test is needed when the ratio test has already failed (ρ = 1); the rule L > 1 converge, L < 1 diverge still applies whenever the limit L exists.

problem: 'Use Raabe's reciprocal aₙ/aₙ₊₁' is loose wording. aₙ/aₙ₊₁ is the reciprocal of the ratio-test quantity aₙ₊₁/aₙ; calling it 'Raabe's reciprocal' can confuse a reader into thinking an extra inversion is needed.
fix: In Raabe's test use the ratio aₙ/aₙ₊₁ — the upside-down version of the ratio-test ratio aₙ₊₁/aₙ — never aₙ₊₁/aₙ.

where: Both formula blocks and the statement of each test
problem: The limits are written only as '→ L' with no statement that n → ∞ and no condition that the limit must exist. If Rₙ (or the log quotient) oscillates and has no limit, neither test gives any conclusion, and the chapter never says so.
fix: Write Rₙ = n(aₙ/aₙ₊₁ − 1) → L as n → ∞, and add: if this limit does not exist (the expression oscillates), the test gives no conclusion. Add the same n → ∞ note to the logarithmic-test formula.
